notes: Too little data + too high LR; model barely moved from baseline.
Healthy loss behavior (not overfit) but WER still regressed -- read as undertraining.
First run to beat baseline. Two variables changed at once vs v3 (full fine-tune + more epochs) -- doesn't isolate which mattered. ~13min on Colab GPU vs v3's ~6.5hr on MPS.

Not a training run -- a manifest cleanup pass, logged here to track dataset provenance over time. Found via manual spot-check (scripts/sample_alignment_check.py) that some LRCLIB-timestamped chunks were badly misaligned with their audio (one off by 16s). Root cause: dataset.py matched LRCLIB lyrics to audio by artist/title text only, no duration check -- a loose YouTube search can return a different edit/upload (wrong video entirely, looped upload, different single cut) whose lyrics text matches but whose timing doesn't. Confirmed via LRCLIB's duration field vs actual downloaded audio duration: 37/81 songs (46%) had a mismatch >5s, up to 647s (Tame Impala 'Dracula' turned out to be a 14-minute interview video, not the song). Dropped all 37. Also: added a 0.25s padding on chunk audio slicing (train.py) to stop clipping word onsets/codas at chunk boundaries, and a filter dropping near-empty/symbol-only segments like placeholder '♪' instrumental-break lines (42/3756 segments, some spanning 20+s). Added a forward-looking duration check in dataset.py (_download_billboard_audio) so future builds reject mismatched songs automatically instead of silently keeping them.

Same method/epochs/lr as v4 -- only changed variable is data quality (data-fixup-1): dropped duration-mismatched songs, filtered near-empty segments, added chunk-boundary padding. Result: baseline 66.2% -> fine-tuned 55.1%, by far the biggest WER win so far (v4 was +2.4pp, this is +11.2pp), isolating that the data bugs were capping WER more than the full-finetune/epoch choice was. Caveat: train_loss collapsed to ~0.03 while eval_loss stayed flat around 1.2-1.3 across all 5 epochs -- classic overfitting on the smaller 34-song train split. The eval WER gain is real (measured on held-out artists), but there's likely headroom left if overfitting is addressed (fewer epochs, early stopping, or more clean data).

Phase 2 ablation: same clean data + 5 epochs as v5, but LoRA instead of full fine-tune, to isolate which drove v4/v5's win. Result: baseline 66.2% -> fine-tuned 58.6% (+7.7pp) -- a real win, but 3.5pp worse than v5's full-finetune result (+11.2pp), so full fine-tuning does have a genuine edge here, not just noise. Notably, LoRA's loss curve is much healthier than v5's (train_loss 0.62 vs v5's 0.03; eval_loss 0.94 vs v5's 1.28 -- LoRA's eval_loss is actually LOWER than full fine-tune's, despite full fine-tune winning on WER). This means eval_loss and WER aren't moving together cleanly at this scale (greedy-decoded WER vs teacher-forced loss, only 10 eval chunks), and more importantly, that v5's 0.03 train_loss means it essentially memorized the 34-song train split -- a shorter full-finetune run (fewer epochs / early stopping) is a more promising next experiment than concluding full fine-tune is simply better.
